concepts.title: A Living Document: Constitution Across Generations

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'A Living Document: Constitution Across Generations' refers to.
questions.a: A constitution written in one era must govern many others, so it must be neither frozen nor flimsy. India's text has endured by adapting: over a hundred amendments, landmark interpretations and steady practice have let the same framework serve a changing society -- the meaning of a living document.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'A Living Document: Constitution Across Generations'.
questions.a: Rigid enough to endure, flexible enough to grow -- a living constitution changes without dying.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Amendment Procedure: Article 368' refers to.
questions.a: Article 368 lets Parliament amend most provisions by a special majority -- more than half the total membership and two-thirds of those present. Some federal features additionally need ratification by half the state legislatures. No provision, however, is formally beyond amendment -- a choice that keeps the text amendable yet hard to touch casually.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Amendment Procedure: Article 368'.
questions.a: Special majority, sometimes plus half the states -- amendment is possible but never cheap.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Amendment Procedure: Article 368' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2 (source: keps209.txt lines 110-220 (amendment procedure, article 368, special majority, ratification by states, comparison with rigid and flexible constitutions))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Basic Structure and Landmark Amendments' refers to.
questions.a: Parliament's amendments collided with the courts. Golak Nath blocked amending rights; Parliament answered with the 24th Amendment; Kesavananda Bharati then ruled that amendments cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure -- democracy, secularism, judicial review, federalism. The 42nd Amendment tried total parliamentary supremacy; Minerva Mills struck its sweep down. Thus courts, not text, drew the final line.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Basic Structure and Landmark Amendments'.
questions.a: Parliament can amend anything but cannot kill the Constitution's identity -- the basic structure doctrine is the living document's spine.

concepts.title: Constitution as an Instrument of Social Change

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Constitution as an Instrument of Social Change' refers to.
questions.a: Amendments have pushed society, not just machinery: the 73rd and 74th Amendments brought panchayats and municipalities into the Constitution, the 86th made elementary education a right, the 101st introduced the goods and services tax. Interpretation too widened rights -- reading life and liberty expansively, recognizing dignity in new spheres.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Constitution as an Instrument of Social Change'.
questions.a: Amendments and interpretations have aimed the Constitution at inequality itself -- law as engine of social transformation.
